meta.title_plain: How a giant metal plane rides on thin air
meta.teaser: Lift, thrust, drag and weight: the four-way tug-of-war that keeps planes up.

page.title: How a giant metal plane rides on thin air
page.sub: The science behind how airplanes fly
page.bigIdea: A plane flies because its wings push air down, and the air pushes back up. The engines just keep it moving fast enough for that to work.

cards.title: A four-way tug-of-war
cards.front: Four forces pull on a plane every second it flies.
cards.back: Weight pulls the plane down. Lift pushes it up. Thrust pushes it forward. Drag holds it back. When all four balance, the plane cruises at a steady speed.
cards.tryit: Hold a book flat on your palm. Gravity pulls it down. Your hand is the lift. Now lower your hand slowly: what wins?

cards.title: Wings turn air downward
cards.front: A wing is a machine for bending air.
cards.back: As air flows past, the wing bends it downward. Newton's third law says the air pushes back up on the wing. Lower pressure above the wing helps too.
cards.tryit: Hold the curved back of a spoon near a gentle stream from the tap. Watch the water bend around it and pull the spoon in.

cards.title: Engines push, wings lift
cards.front: Surprise: the engines don't hold the plane up.
cards.back: Engines only beat drag. A big airliner's engines push with about a fifth of its weight. The wings do the lifting. Gliders have no engine and still fly!
cards.tryit: Fold a paper plane. Throw it once gently and once hard. Your arm is the engine. Which throw glides further?

cards.title: Tilt it, but not too much
cards.front: Pointing the wing up a little gives more lift.
cards.back: The wing's tilt is the angle of attack. More tilt, more lift, until about 15 degrees. Then air peels off the top and lift drops. That's a stall.
cards.tryit: Bend up the back edges of your paper plane's wings a little. Throw it. Now bend them a lot. Does it swoop up, then drop?

cards.title: Roll, pitch and yaw
cards.front: In 1903 the Wright brothers' first flight lasted 12 seconds. Their big trick was steering.
cards.back: Ailerons on the wingtips roll the plane. The elevator on the tail tips the nose up or down. The rudder swings the nose left or right.
cards.tryit: Bend one wing's back edge up and the other down on your paper plane. Throw it. Which way does it roll?

words.d: The upward push on a wing as air flows past it.
The forward push from engines or propellers.
The air resisting a plane as it moves forward.
How much a wing is tilted up against the oncoming air.
A sudden loss of lift when a wing tilts too far.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a plane's engines?
opts: To lift the plane straight up
To beat drag and push it forward
quiz.hint: Think about gliders. They have no engine at all.
quiz.why: The wings make the lift, so the engines only need to overcome drag and keep the plane moving.

quiz.q: How does a wing make lift?
opts: It turns air downward, so the air pushes it up
It is lighter than air, like a balloon
quiz.hint: Remember Newton: every push has an equal push back.
quiz.why: The wing pushes air down, and Newton's third law means the air pushes the wing up.

opts: The plane runs out of fuel
The wing tilts too far and loses lift
quiz.hint: Think about your paper plane with its wing edges bent up a lot.
quiz.why: Past the critical angle, air peels off the wing's top and lift drops, even with engines running.

quiz.q: Which part tips the nose up or down?
quiz.hint: It lives on the tail and its name sounds like going up and down floors.
quiz.why: The elevator on the tail controls pitch, pointing the nose up or down.

page.think: A tennis ball with topspin dips because air pushes on it. Where else in your games or sports do you think air is pushing things up, down or sideways?
